gap: No result ChatGPT got states that The Solar Lab measured a 37 W inverter-on idle draw and 83% efficiency on ChatGPT's own pick, the PECRON F3000LFP. With those figures the PECRON's 3,072 Wh lasts about 11.4 h, short of 12 h, under ChatGPT's own assumption of an 800 W pump at 25% duty. RunTimeFit's '~16 hours' left idle draw out. Notebookcheck measured the BLUETTI Elite 300 at 2,650 Wh delivered at about 200 W, and named-tester figures put the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at about 17 h and the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus at about 15 h on the same assumption.
standout_why: Compared against the cited pages runtimefit.com (says outright that its runtimes come from maker specs and leave idle draw out), outagereadyhq.com ('We have not run these units with a sump pump ourselves'; assumes 85% usable) and homebatteryreport.com ('We have not lab-tested these units'), plus amphourly.com from the top results (assumes 85% usable, no idle draw). testedwatts.com (cited) would not load because of a certificate error, so it is unchecked. solarpowerauditor.com was a result but was not cited. It has Scott Caine's measured idle and usable Wh for the DELTA Pro 3 and F3800 Plus only. It has nothing for the PECRON or the Elite 300, and it never works out the 12-hour sump case. None of these pages has a measured idle draw or measured usable energy for the PECRON F3000LFP, which is the product ChatGPT recommended.
decides: This changes the pick. The PECRON F3000LFP that ChatGPT recommended loses about 333 Wh to its 37 W idle draw over the 9 hours the pump is off, so it falls short of 12 h at 25% duty with an 800 W pump (about 11.4 h). Even with RunTimeFit's own 650 W pump it reaches only about 13.7 h, not 16 h. On named-tester measurements the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the safe 12-hour choice: Scott Caine measured 3,772 Wh usable and 34 W idle (about 16.9 h), and The Solar Lab ran it at 5,100 W surge for nearly a minute. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus is next (3,448 Wh, 38 W idle, about 15.3 h). The Elite 300 gets past 12 h on energy, but its 4,800 W lifting rating applies to resistive loads only. Nobody measured a motor start on any candidate, so pump starting stays a spec-sheet question. None of this changes the literal 13 HP reading, which no portable station covers.

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on, no load (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: Pecron F3000LFP portable power station review · The Solar Lab
findings.note: Measured with only the inverter on, after charging to 100% and draining. The page shows no review date or author. Over the 9 h an 800 W pump is off at 25% duty: 9 × 37 = 333 Wh.

findings.label: AC discharge efficiency (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 83% at a sustained 3,600 W, full to empty
findings.source_title: Pecron F3000LFP portable power station review · The Solar Lab
findings.note: 3,072 Wh × 0.83 ≈ 2,550 Wh delivered. Our arithmetic, 800 W pump at 25% duty: per hour 0.25 × 800 / 0.83 + 0.75 × 37 = 241 + 27.75 = 268.7 Wh, so 3,072 / 268.7 ≈ 11.4 h. With RunTimeFit's 650 W: 195.8 + 27.75 = 223.5 Wh per hour, about 13.7 h (RunTimeFit says about 16 h). The efficiency was measured at full load, and low-load efficiency may differ.

findings.label: Surge hold (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 4,500 W for about 10 s, then tripped and needed a restart
findings.source_title: Pecron F3000LFP portable power station review · The Solar Lab
findings.note: The test appliance is not named. This was not a motor-start test.
